claim: A proteomic analysis of gastrocnemius muscle from 73 genetically distinct inbred mouse strains of the HMDP was performed.
source: To begin to understand how variations in the genome drive changes in the skeletal muscle proteome, we performed a proteomic analysis of gastrocnemius muscle from 73 inbred mouse strains of the HMDP that were fed a chow diet and housed under identical environmental conditions (n=2–4; 161 mice).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the experimental design and sample size.

claim: The proteomic analysis quantified 5350 proteins with 4027 quantified in >50 mice and 2069 proteins quantified in all 161 animals.
source: Peptides were analysed by 2D-liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (2D-LC-MS/MS) resulting in the quantification of 5350 proteins with 4027 quantified in >50 mice and 2069 proteins quantified in all 161 animals (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct quantification results from mass spectrometry analysis are reported, and Figure 1B shows the number of proteins identified.

claim: Median intra-strain coefficient of variation was 9.2% while inter-strain coefficient was significantly larger.
source: Median intra-strain coefficient of variation was 9.2% while inter-strain coefficient was significantly larger, suggesting reproducible quantification and genetically driven variation in the proteome was captured in the data (Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical measurements of variation are provided with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Local SNPs were associated to the abundance of 527 unique proteins (cis-regulation).
source: We identified significant cis-regulation of the proteome with local SNPs associated to the abundance of 527 unique proteins (±10 Mb of gene; local adjusted p<1 × 10−4) and trans-regulation with distant SNPs (>10 Mb of the gene or on a different chromosome) associated to the abundance of 170 unique proteins (global adjusted p<5 × 10−8) (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Results from pQTL mapping analysis are reported with statistical thresholds.

claim: Distant SNPs were associated to the abundance of 170 unique proteins (trans-regulation).
source: We identified significant cis-regulation of the proteome with local SNPs associated to the abundance of 527 unique proteins (±10 Mb of gene; local adjusted p<1 × 10−4) and trans-regulation with distant SNPs (>10 Mb of the gene or on a different chromosome) associated to the abundance of 170 unique proteins (global adjusted p<5 × 10−8) (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Results from pQTL mapping analysis are reported with statistical thresholds.

claim: A cis-pQTL on chromosome 1 (lead SNP rs31934459) is associated to the abundance of RPL7 and is also a trans-pQTL for RPL19 and RPL23.
source: Here, we show a cis-pQTL on chromosome 1 (lead SNP rs31934459) is associated to the abundance of RPL7 and is also a trans-pQTL for RPL19 and RPL23.
evidence: Specific genetic associations are identified from the pQTL analysis.

claim: RPL7, RPL19, and RPL23 are correlated in abundance and form a co-regulated network with other 60S ribosomal proteins.
source: These proteins are correlated in abundance and form a co-regulated network with other 60S ribosomal proteins suggesting genetic variants regulating RPL7 abundance subsequently regulate protein complex stability/assembly (Figure 1F and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Correlation analysis and network visualization support this claim.

claim: A cis-pQTL associated with MOCS2 is also a trans-pQTL for eight proteins all members of mitochondrial complex V.
source: A cis-pQTL associated with MOCS2 is also a trans-pQTL for eight proteins all members of mitochondrial complex V (Figure 1G).
evidence: Genetic association results are reported with reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Patients with mutations in MOCS1 that result in mild molybdenum cofactor deficiency also display reduced mitochondrial respiration.
source: Patients with mutations in MOCS1 that result in mild molybdenum cofactor deficiency also display reduced mitochondrial respiration suggesting a link between molybdopterin biosynthesis and ATP production (Grings et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grings et al., 2019.

claim: Among the 527 proteins with a cis-pQTL association, 212 had an intragenic association.
source: Among the 527 proteins with a cis-pQTL association, 212 had an intragenic association.
evidence: Quantitative results from variant effect analysis are reported.

claim: Non-coding SNPs in the fifth and sixth intron of Acadl were cis-pQTLs for ACADL.
source: For example, non-coding SNPs in the fifth and sixth intron of Acadl were cis-pQTLs for ACADL (Figure 1H).
evidence: Specific genetic associations are identified with reference to Figure 1H.

claim: The rs32746574 variant (GG >AA; R338C) was associated with significantly lower abundance of EPHX1.
source: We also identified 14 missense variants as pQTLs such as the rs32746574 variant (GG >AA; R338C), which was associated with significantly lower abundance of EPHX1 (Figure 1I).
evidence: Genetic association with protein abundance is reported with reference to Figure 1I.

claim: The R338C mutation in EPHX1 was found to be deleterious (PROVEAN score: –5.6).
source: The R338C mutation was found to be deleterious (PROVEAN score: –5.6) (Choi and Chan, 2015), destabilizing (FoldX:+1.1 ΔG) (Delgado et al., 2019) and possibly damaging (PolyPhen2 HumDiv: 0.62) (Adzhubei et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Computational prediction tools were used to assess the mutation effect, with citations to the methods.

claim: The R338C mutation in EPHX1 is destabilizing (FoldX:+1.1 ΔG).
source: The R338C mutation was found to be deleterious (PROVEAN score: –5.6) (Choi and Chan, 2015), destabilizing (FoldX:+1.1 ΔG) (Delgado et al., 2019) and possibly damaging (PolyPhen2 HumDiv: 0.62) (Adzhubei et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Computational prediction tools were used to assess the mutation effect, with citations to the methods.

claim: The R338C mutation in EPHX1 is possibly damaging (PolyPhen2 HumDiv: 0.62).
source: The R338C mutation was found to be deleterious (PROVEAN score: –5.6) (Choi and Chan, 2015), destabilizing (FoldX:+1.1 ΔG) (Delgado et al., 2019) and possibly damaging (PolyPhen2 HumDiv: 0.62) (Adzhubei et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Computational prediction tools were used to assess the mutation effect, with citations to the methods.

claim: R338C increases the flexibility of EPHX1 due to the missing interaction (hydrogen bond) between R338 and Y291.
source: R338C increases the flexibility of EPHX1 due to the missing interaction (hydrogen bond) between R338 and Y291 (Figure 1J).
evidence: Structural analysis results are reported with reference to Figure 1J.

claim: A locus on chromosome 7 contained cis-pQTLs associated to MCEE that were shared with fasting glucose in mice subject to high-fat/high-sugar feeding.
source: For example, a locus on chromosome 7 contained cis-pQTLs associated to MCEE that were shared with fasting glucose in mice subject to high-fat/high-sugar feeding (Figure 2C).
evidence: Integration of genetic and phenotypic data identified this association.

claim: Homozygous allelic variation of SNPs were associated to MCEE protein abundance and also a trend for greater visceral adiposity and fasting glucose on a chow diet.
source: Homozygous allelic variation of SNPs were associated to MCEE protein abundance and also a trend for greater visceral adiposity and fasting glucose on a chow diet (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: Allelic association analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 2D-E.

claim: MCEE functions as a methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase important for propionyl-CoA metabolism.
source: MCEE functions as a methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase important for propionyl-CoA metabolism.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical function.

claim: Rare autosomal recessive missense mutations in MCEE have been identified in patients with methylmalonic aciduria.
source: Rare autosomal recessive missense mutations in MCEE have been identified in patients with methylmalonic aciduria (Bikker et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bikker et al., 2006.

claim: Intragenic SNPs in both OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 genes were associated with several cardiometabolic parameters of adiposity including percentage body fat, retroperitoneal fat mass, circulating free fatty acids, HDL, and cholesterol.
source: Intragenic SNPs in both genes were associated with several cardiometabolic parameters of adiposity including percentage body fat assessed by nuclear magnetic resonance, retroperitoneal fat mass, circulating free fatty acids, HDL, and cholesterol.
evidence: Genetic association results with multiple phenotypes are reported.

claim: The abundance of OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 were positively correlated to several cardiometabolic traits.
source: Furthermore, the abundance of OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 were positively correlated to several of these traits, and homozygous allelic variation of SNPs in both the Ociad1 and Ociad2 loci were associated to protein abundance and cholesterol (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 2F-G.

claim: Recent data have revealed a role for OCIAD1/2 in mitochondrial complex III assembly.
source: Very little is known about the functions of OCIAD1/2 but recent data have revealed a role in mitochondrial complex III assembly (Le Vasseur et al., 2021) and human GWAS analysis has identified variants in both the OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 loci are associated with susceptibility to type 2 diabetes (Vujkovic et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Le Vasseur et al., 2021.

claim: Human GWAS analysis has identified variants in both the OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 loci are associated with susceptibility to type 2 diabetes.
source: Very little is known about the functions of OCIAD1/2 but recent data have revealed a role in mitochondrial complex III assembly (Le Vasseur et al., 2021) and human GWAS analysis has identified variants in both the OCIAD1 and OCIAD2 loci are associated with susceptibility to type 2 diabetes (Vujkovic et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vujkovic et al., 2020.

claim: Genetic variants associated to the abundance of SLC37A4 co-localize to fasting glucose and fat pad mass in mice fed a chow diet.
source: We also identified genetic variants associated to the abundance of the ER resident glucose-6-phosphate transporter SLC37A4 that co-localize to fasting glucose and fat pad mass in mice fed a chow diet (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: Genetic association results are reported with reference to Figures 2H-I.

claim: SLC37A4 has enhanced expression in the liver, gut, and kidney, and plays a role in the regulation of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
source: SLC37A4 has enhanced expression in the liver, gut, and kidney, and plays a role in the regulation of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, however, its role in skeletal muscle metabolism has been comparatively less studied.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about SLC37A4 function and expression.

claim: Patients with mutations in SLC37A4 present with several metabolic complications, particularly hepatomegaly and enlarged kidneys due to the accumulation of glycogen but also often have signs of dyslipidaemia and hypoglycemia.
source: Patients with mutations in SLC37A4 present with several metabolic complications, particularly hepatomegaly and enlarged kidneys due to the accumulation of glycogen but also often have signs of dyslipidaemia and hypoglycemia.
evidence: This is a statement of established clinical knowledge about SLC37A4 mutations.

claim: 300 proteins were positively or negatively associated to lean mass (–0.3 < r > 0.6, p<0.05).
source: Using supervised multivariate and pairwise correlation analysis, we identified 300 proteins positively or negatively associated to lean mass (–0.3 < r > 0.6, p<0.05) (Figure 2K).
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported with statistical thresholds and reference to Figure 2K.

claim: Proteins involved in translation including ribosomal subunits and elongation initiation factors were positively correlated with lean mass.
source: Proteins involved in translation including ribosomal subunits and elongation initiation factors were positively correlated while we observed several extracellular matrix proteins including collagens and cathepsins to be negatively correlated with lean mass.
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: Several extracellular matrix proteins including collagens and cathepsins were negatively correlated with lean mass.
source: Proteins involved in translation including ribosomal subunits and elongation initiation factors were positively correlated while we observed several extracellular matrix proteins including collagens and cathepsins to be negatively correlated with lean mass.
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: INMT, MOCS2, and TACC2 show negative correlations with lean mass.
source: Allelic variations were integrated to highlight several trends such as negative correlations between INMT, MOCS2, and TACC2 versus lean mass (Figure 2L–N), where alleles which reduced protein abundance (rs49460035, rs28162611, and rs32292483) generally displayed lower lean mass (Figure 2O–Q).
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 2L-N.

claim: Alleles which reduced INMT, MOCS2, and TACC2 protein abundance generally displayed lower lean mass.
source: Allelic variations were integrated to highlight several trends such as negative correlations between INMT, MOCS2, and TACC2 versus lean mass (Figure 2L–N), where alleles which reduced protein abundance (rs49460035, rs28162611, and rs32292483) generally displayed lower lean mass (Figure 2O–Q).
evidence: Allelic association analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 2O-Q.

claim: A negative correlation exists between UFC1 abundance and lean mass.
source: Our data identified a negative correlation between UFC1, lean mass, and plasma cholesterol.
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: A negative correlation exists between UFC1 abundance and plasma cholesterol.
source: Our data identified a negative correlation between UFC1, lean mass, and plasma cholesterol.
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: UFC1 is the E2 ligase for the post-translational modification of ubiquitin-fold modifier 1 (UFM1) to target proteins through UFMylation.
source: UFC1 is the E2 ligase for the post-translational modification of ubiquitin-fold modifier 1 (UFM1) to target proteins through UFMylation.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical function.

claim: Negative correlations exist between MPZ and plasma cholesterol/triacylglycerols (TAGs).
source: We also identified negative correlations between MPZ and plasma cholesterol/triacylglycerols (TAGs).
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is associated with reduced expression of Mpz, myelin abnormalities, and several defects in lipid metabolism.
source: It is unclear if MPZ plays a causative role in the regulation of lipid metabolism, however diabetic peripheral neuropathy is associated with reduced expression of Mpz, myelin abnormalities, and several defects in lipid metabolism (Cermenati et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cermenati et al., 2012.

claim: Positive correlations were found between BPNT1 and plasma insulin, HOMA-IR, and visceral fat.
source: Positive correlations were found between BPNT1 and plasma insulin, HOMA-IR, and visceral fat while also negatively correlated with plasma cholesterol, TAGs, and lean mass.
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: BPNT1 is negatively correlated with plasma cholesterol, TAGs, and lean mass.
source: Positive correlations were found between BPNT1 and plasma insulin, HOMA-IR, and visceral fat while also negatively correlated with plasma cholesterol, TAGs, and lean mass.
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: BPNT1 is involved in phosphatidylinositol phosphate and adenosine phosphate metabolism.
source: BPNT1 is involved in phosphatidylinositol phosphate and adenosine phosphate metabolism.
evidence: This is a statement of established biochemical function.

claim: Mice lacking Bpnt1 display severe liver defects.
source: Mice lacking Bpnt1 display severe liver defects but the role of this enzyme in whole body energy metabolism and insulin sensitivity is currently unknown (Hudson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hudson et al., 2013.

claim: An overall negative correlation exists between the abundance of EPHX1 and HOMA-IR, visceral fat, plasma insulin, and cholesterol.
source: Finally, we observed an overall negative correlation between the abundance of EPHX1 and HOMA-IR, visceral fat, plasma insulin, and cholesterol.
evidence: Correlation analysis results are reported.

claim: 27 individual recombinant AAV serotype 6 viral vectors expressing shRNA (rAAV6:shRNAs) were generated to knock down target proteins.
source: We focused on proteins with negative associations to lean mass, grip strength, or other metabolic traits, and generated a total of 27 individual recombinant AAV serotype 6 viral vectors expressing shRNA (rAAV6:shRNAs) to knock down the expression of these proteins in an arrayed fashion.
evidence: The experimental design and methods are explicitly described.

claim: Proteomics analysis of hµMs quantified 17/27 targets with 13 targets significantly reduced in abundance by rAAV6:shRNA.
source: Following this protocol, hµMs were analysed by proteomics which quantified 17/27 targets with 13 targets significantly reduced in abundance by rAAV6:shRNA (Figure 4B).
evidence: Proteomic analysis results are reported with reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of UFC1, MCEE, TOM1L2, and SH3BGR resulted in significant increases in maximum force production during tetanic contractions.
source: Knockdown of UFC1, MCEE, TOM1L2, and SH3BGR was confirmed at the protein level and resulted in significant increases in maximum force production during the tetanic contractions (Figure 4C).
evidence: Functional assay results are reported with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: Knockdown of UFC1 increased force production during the fatigue protocol.
source: Remarkably, knockdown of UFC1 increased force production during the fatigue protocol.
evidence: Functional assay results are reported.

claim: Knockdown of CNST protected against fatigue.
source: Knockdown of CNST also protected against fatigue, but we were unable to identify CNST in the proteomics analyses to confirm knockdown.
evidence: Functional assay results are reported, though knockdown was not confirmed by proteomics.

claim: At 25 weeks of age, there was a significant increase in conjugated and free UFM1, UFC1, and UFSP2 in gastrocnemius skeletal muscles of SOD1(G37R) mice.
source: At 25 weeks of age, we observed a significant increase in conjugated and free UFM1, UFC1, and UFSP2 (a deUFMylase) in gastrocnemius skeletal muscles of SOD1(G37R) mice, which was independent of any changes in the abundance of BiP chaperone as a marker of ER stress (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Western blot analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 5A-B.

claim: The increase in UFMylation components in SOD1(G37R) mice was independent of any changes in the abundance of BiP chaperone as a marker of ER stress.
source: At 25 weeks of age, we observed a significant increase in conjugated and free UFM1, UFC1, and UFSP2 (a deUFMylase) in gastrocnemius skeletal muscles of SOD1(G37R) mice, which was independent of any changes in the abundance of BiP chaperone as a marker of ER stress (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Western blot analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 5A-B.

claim: UFMylation is up-regulated in a mouse model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: We show UFMylation is up-regulated in a mouse model of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease that involves muscle atrophy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Following 12 weeks of transduction with rAAV6:shUFC1, there were significant reductions in the abundance of UFC1 and conjugated UFM1.
source: Following 12 weeks of transduction, we observed significant reductions in the abundance of UFC1 and conjugated UFM1 (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Western blot analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 5D-E.

claim: Knockdown of UFC1 resulted in a subtle but significant increase in whole muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) but no change in muscle mass.
source: There was a subtle but significant increase in whole muscle cross-sectional area (CSA) but no change in muscle mass (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: Morphometric analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 5G-H.

claim: Knockdown of UFC1 increased specific force production in response to a single twitch contraction (sPt).
source: Knockdown of UFC1 increased specific force production in response to a single twitch contraction (sPt) and generated almost a doubling of peak force (sPo), normalized to CSA (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: Ex vivo muscle function testing results are reported with reference to Figures 5I-J.

claim: Knockdown of UFC1 generated almost a doubling of peak tetanic force (sPo), normalized to CSA.
source: Knockdown of UFC1 increased specific force production in response to a single twitch contraction (sPt) and generated almost a doubling of peak force (sPo), normalized to CSA (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: Ex vivo muscle function testing results are reported with reference to Figures 5I-J.

claim: Both the absolute and specific tetanic force increased across all stimulation frequencies tested following knockdown of UFC1.
source: Furthermore, both the absolute and specific tetanic force increased across all stimulation frequencies tested following knockdown of UFC1 (Figure 5K–L).
evidence: Ex vivo muscle function testing results are reported with reference to Figures 5K-L.

claim: In vivo knockdown of UFMylation increased contraction force.
source: Furthermore, in vivo knockdown of UFMylation increased contraction force, implicating its role as a negative regulator of skeletal muscle function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5I-L.

claim: There were no differences in the abundance of myosin isoforms following knockdown of UFC1.
source: First, we analysed fiber-type composition of TA muscles by immunofluorescence microscopy of which revealed no differences in the abundance of myosin isoforms but there was a trend for a decrease in the total number of muscle fibers following knockdown of UFC1 (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 6A-C.

claim: There was a trend for a decrease in the total number of muscle fibers following knockdown of UFC1.
source: First, we analysed fiber-type composition of TA muscles by immunofluorescence microscopy of which revealed no differences in the abundance of myosin isoforms but there was a trend for a decrease in the total number of muscle fibers following knockdown of UFC1 (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 6A-C.

claim: Proteomic analysis of EDL muscles quantified 5909 proteins of which 573 were regulated in abundance following knockdown of UFC1.
source: Next, we performed a proteomic analysis of EDL muscles which quantified 5909 proteins of which 573 were regulated in abundance following knockdown of UFC1 (Figure 6D and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Proteomic analysis results are reported with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: The top up-regulated pathways following UFC1 knockdown included proteins associated with translation, muscle contraction, and signal recognition particle (SRP)-mediated translocation to the ER.
source: The top up-regulated pathways included proteins associated with translation, muscle contraction, and signal recognition particle (SRP)-mediated translocation to the ER, while down-regulation was observed in immune-related pathways and cell surface interactions (Figure 6E).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis results are reported with reference to Figure 6E.

claim: Down-regulation was observed in immune-related pathways and cell surface interactions following UFC1 knockdown.
source: The top up-regulated pathways included proteins associated with translation, muscle contraction, and signal recognition particle (SRP)-mediated translocation to the ER, while down-regulation was observed in immune-related pathways and cell surface interactions (Figure 6E).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis results are reported with reference to Figure 6E.

claim: The up-regulation of contractile proteins following knockdown of UFC1 includes fast-type Troponin T (TNNT3), which had the largest fold change (>2.5-fold).
source: The up-regulation of contractile proteins following knockdown of UFC1 includes fast-type Troponin T (TNNT3), which binds tropomyosin, and the protein with the largest fold change (>2.5-fold) (Figure 6F).
evidence: Proteomic analysis results are reported with reference to Figure 6F.

claim: The most up-regulated proteins in the translational machinery following UFC1 knockdown were SRPA/B of the SRP complex, SSR1/2/3/4 of the TRAP complex, and SEC61A/B.
source: The most up-regulated proteins in the translational machinery were SRPA/B of the SRP complex, SSR1/2/3/4 of the TRAP complex, and SEC61A/B (Figure 6G).
evidence: Proteomic analysis results are reported with reference to Figure 6G.

claim: There was a trend for increased RPL31 following UFC1 knockdown, which mediates binding of SRP to the ribosome.
source: We also observed a trend for increased RPL31 which mediates binding of SRP to the ribosome (Pech et al., 2010).
evidence: Proteomic analysis results are reported with citation to Pech et al., 2010 for RPL31 function.

claim: The core subunits of the proteasome, and atrogenes including TRIM63 and ASB2 were not regulated following knockdown of UFC1.
source: The core subunits of the proteasome, and atrogenes including TRIM63 and ASB2 were not regulated following knockdown of UFC1 (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Proteomic analysis results are reported.

claim: The proteasome activating complex PSME1/2 was down-regulated with UFC1 knockdown.
source: However, the proteasome activating complex PSME1/2 was down-regulated with UFC1 knockdown and western blotting revealed a decrease in K48-linked ubiquitination (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: Proteomic and western blot analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 6H-I.

claim: Western blotting revealed a decrease in K48-linked ubiquitination following UFC1 knockdown.
source: However, the proteasome activating complex PSME1/2 was down-regulated with UFC1 knockdown and western blotting revealed a decrease in K48-linked ubiquitination (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: Western blot analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 6H-I.

claim: A complex regulation of autophagy-associated proteins was observed following UFC1 knockdown, including up-regulation of GABARAP and ATG3, and down-regulation of ATG4A, WIPI1, and SQSTM1.
source: We also observed a complex regulation of autophagy-associated proteins such as up-regulation of GABARAP and ATG3, and down-regulation of ATG4A, WIPI1, and SQSTM1, the latter which trended to decrease by >1.8-fold with both western blotting and proteomics (Figure 6H–I and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Proteomic and western blot analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 6H-I.

claim: SQSTM1 trended to decrease by >1.8-fold with both western blotting and proteomics following UFC1 knockdown.
source: We also observed a complex regulation of autophagy-associated proteins such as up-regulation of GABARAP and ATG3, and down-regulation of ATG4A, WIPI1, and SQSTM1, the latter which trended to decrease by >1.8-fold with both western blotting and proteomics (Figure 6H–I and Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Proteomic and western blot analysis results are reported with reference to Figures 6H-I.

claim: UFMylation plays a role in skeletal muscle function via modulating proteostasis mechanisms and contractile proteins.
source: Taken together, our data reveal that UFMylation is regulated during atrophy and plays a role in skeletal muscle function via modulating proteostasis mechanisms and contractile proteins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The most abundant target of UFMylation in mammalian cell culture validated by two independent studies is RPL26.
source: However, the most abundant target of UFMylation in mammalian cell culture and validated by two independent studies is RPL26, a ribosomal-associated protein in close proximity to the interaction sites of RPL31 and the SEC61 complex (Walczak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Walczak et al., 2019 and Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The UFM1 E3 ligase, UFL1, is targeted to the ER via UFBP1 (DDRGK1).
source: Indeed, the UFM1 E3 ligase, UFL1, is targeted to the ER via UFBP1 (DDRGK1) (Wang et al., 2020), and UFMylation is required for ER-phagy (Liang et al., 2020) and ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) (Walczak et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: UFMylation is required for ER-phagy.
source: Indeed, the UFM1 E3 ligase, UFL1, is targeted to the ER via UFBP1 (DDRGK1) (Wang et al., 2020), and UFMylation is required for ER-phagy (Liang et al., 2020) and ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) (Walczak et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Liang et al., 2020.

claim: UFMylation is required for ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD).
source: Indeed, the UFM1 E3 ligase, UFL1, is targeted to the ER via UFBP1 (DDRGK1) (Wang et al., 2020), and UFMylation is required for ER-phagy (Liang et al., 2020) and ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD) (Walczak et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walczak et al., 2019.

claim: RPL26 UFMylation promotes the degradation of a translocation-arrested ER protein.
source: Mechanistically, RPL26 UFMylation promotes the degradation of a translocation-arrested ER protein and up-regulation may play a role in enhanced secretory flux (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: Up-regulation of RPL26 UFMylation may play a role in enhanced secretory flux.
source: Mechanistically, RPL26 UFMylation promotes the degradation of a translocation-arrested ER protein and up-regulation may play a role in enhanced secretory flux (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claim: UFMylation plays a positive role in ER stress and cellular protection.
source: Hence, UFMylation plays a positive role in ER stress and cellular protection, and it is potentially paradoxical that reducing UFMylation can improve muscle contractile function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature about UFMylation function.

claim: Mutations in UFSP2 have been identified which increase UFMylation and result in musculoskeletal dysplasia.
source: In further support of a negative association of UFMylation and muscle function, mutations in UFSP2 have been identified which increase UFMylation and result in musculoskeletal dysplasia (Watson et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Watson et al., 2015 and Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: The expression of UFC1 is up-regulated in skeletal myocytes differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells derived from familial ALS (C9ORF72 mutations).
source: Furthermore, the expression of UFC1 is also up-regulated in skeletal myocytes differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells derived from familial ALS (C9ORF72 mutations) (Lynch et al., 2021), and the expression of UBA5, the E1 ligase for UFMylation has recently been associated with Becker muscular dystrophy (Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lynch et al., 2021.

claim: The expression of UBA5, the E1 ligase for UFMylation has recently been associated with Becker muscular dystrophy.
source: Furthermore, the expression of UFC1 is also up-regulated in skeletal myocytes differentiated from induced pluripotent stem cells derived from familial ALS (C9ORF72 mutations) (Lynch et al., 2021), and the expression of UBA5, the E1 ligase for UFMylation has recently been associated with Becker muscular dystrophy (Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2021.

claim: Genetic ablation of UFMylation in cell culture reduces viral-mediated interferon production.
source: Interestingly, genetic ablation of UFMylation in cell culture reduces viral-mediated interferon production and correlates with our observed down-regulation of proteins involved in the innate immune response following UFC1 knockdown suggesting an overall reduction in inflammation (Snider et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Snider et al., 2022.

claim: Skeletal muscle makes up 30–40% of an adult human's body mass.
source: Skeletal muscle makes up 30–40% of an adult human's body mass and is vital not just for breathing and movement, but also for metabolism and longevity.
evidence: This is a statement of established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The maintenance of muscle function is one of the best predictors for overall health.
source: The maintenance of muscle function is one of the best predictors for overall health, with sarcopenia being the major contributor of age-associated frailty (McGregor et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McGregor et al., 2014.

claim: Sarcopenia is the major contributor of age-associated frailty.
source: The maintenance of muscle function is one of the best predictors for overall health, with sarcopenia being the major contributor of age-associated frailty (McGregor et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McGregor et al., 2014.

claim: Systems genetics is a population-based approach that links genetic variation to complex traits.
source: Systems genetics is a population-based approach that links genetic variation to complex traits (Baliga et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baliga et al., 2017.

claim: Recent large-scale plasma proteomic studies in human populations have begun to unravel complex genetic variations and their contribution to proteome diversity and disease-relevant phenotypes.
source: Recent large-scale plasma proteomic studies in human populations have begun to unravel complex genetic variations and their contribution to proteome diversity and disease-relevant phenotypes (Suhre et al., 2017; Benson et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2018; Emilsson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The use of genetic reference panels (GRPs) enables accurate control of the environment, breeding patterns, and access to a range of tissues for molecular analysis.
source: However, unlike studies in humans, the use of genetic reference panels (GRPs) enables accurate control of the environment, breeding patterns, and access to a range of tissues for molecular analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of GRPs as an experimental system.

claim: Systems genetic analyses incorporating transcriptomics, lipidomics, and/or metabolomics in GRPs have led to the discovery of a range of novel regulators of complex phenotypes.
source: Systems genetic analyses incorporating transcriptomics, lipidomics, and/or metabolomics in GRPs have led to the discovery of a range of novel regulators of complex phenotypes ranging from insulin resistance (Parks et al., 2015), insulin secretion (Keller et al., 2019), atherosclerosis (Bennett et al., 2015), lipid metabolism (Jha et al., 2018a; Jha et al., 2018b; Linke et al., 2020), cardiac hypertrophy (Rau et al., 2015), cardiac diastolic dysfunction (Cao et al., 2022), and many more.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The inclusion of proteomics into systems genetic analysis provides information on an important biological layer.
source: The inclusion of proteomics into systems genetic analysis provides information on an important biological layer and has been performed in a range of GRPs including yeast (Foss et al., 2007; Picotti et al., 2013; Parts et al., 2014), worms (Singh et al., 2016), fruit fly (Okada et al., 2016), plants such as maize (Hu et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2019), and several livestock such as cattle (Boudon et al., 2020) and pig (Bovo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies across different organisms.

claim: The use of proteomics to analyse the liver proteome of mouse GRPs has been used to analyse the BxD panel, the Hybrid Mouse Diversity Panel (HMDP), and cohorts of the Collaborative Cross/Diversity Outbred (CC/DO).
source: The use of proteomics to analyse the liver proteome of mouse GRPs has also gained popularity and been used to analyse the BxD panel (Wu et al., 2014; Williams et al., 2016), the Hybrid Mouse Diversity Panel (HMDP) (Ghazalpour et al., 2011; Parker et al., 2019), and cohorts of the Collaborative Cross/Diversity Outbred (CC/DO) (Chick et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Several studies have performed proteomic analysis of additional tissues from cohorts of the BXD and CC/DO and include further phenotypic associations.
source: More recently, several studies have performed proteomic analysis of additional tissues from cohorts of the BXD (Williams et al., 2018) and CC/DO (Xiao et al., 2022) and include further phenotypic associations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Williams et al., 2018 and Xiao et al., 2022.

claim: Functional screening of genetic perturbations with high-throughput phenotypic measurements have identified novel regulators of muscle biology and disease.
source: Functional screening of genetic perturbations with high-throughput phenotypic measurements have identified novel regulators of muscle biology and disease. These include forward genetic mutagenesis screens to identify regulators of skeletal muscle development and locomotion in zebrafish (Birely et al., 2005; Horstick et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2013; Bennett et al., 2018) and worms (Beron et al., 2015), RNAi screening of muscle size and function in fruit fly (Kao et al., 2021; Graca et al., 2021), and CRISPR/Cas9 screening of muscle cells to identify regulators of myogenesis and cell survival in dystrophy models (Bi et al., 2017; Lek et al., 2020; Ashoti et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Mutations in ACS1 are associated with muscular atrophy.
source: Targets of UFMylation include nuclear proteins Histone H4 (Qin et al., 2019), MRE11 (Lee et al., 2021), and ACS1 (Yoo et al., 2014) with the latter particularly relevant to the current study given mutations in ACS1 are associated with muscular atrophy (Davignon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davignon et al., 2016.

claim: Targets of UFMylation include nuclear proteins Histone H4, MRE11, and ACS1.
source: Targets of UFMylation include nuclear proteins Histone H4 (Qin et al., 2019), MRE11 (Lee et al., 2021), and ACS1 (Yoo et al., 2014) with the latter particularly relevant to the current study given mutations in ACS1 are associated with muscular atrophy (Davignon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Qin et al., 2019, Lee et al., 2021, and Yoo et al., 2014.

claim: RPL26 is a ribosomal-associated protein in close proximity to the interaction sites of RPL31 and the SEC61 complex.
source: However, the most abundant target of UFMylation in mammalian cell culture and validated by two independent studies is RPL26, a ribosomal-associated protein in close proximity to the interaction sites of RPL31 and the SEC61 complex (Walczak et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Walczak et al., 2019 and Wang et al., 2020.

claim: RPL26 was not significantly regulated following UFC1 knockdown.
source: While RPL26 was not significantly regulated following UFC1 knockdown, it is possible that the UFMylation status of RPL26 was altered.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the proteomic analysis.

claim: An acute reduction in UFMylation may lead to proteome compensatory remodelling and up-regulation of translational machinery which provide later benefits to muscle function.
source: One potential explanation is an acute reduction in UFMylation leads to proteome compensatory remodelling and up-regulation of translational machinery which provide later benefits to muscle function.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative explanation for the observed results.

claim: The positive enrichment of ribosomal subunits including RPL31, and SRP co-translational factors (SSR1/3, SEC61α, SRPRB) located in close proximity to RPL26 suggests an involvement of UFMylation in this process.
source: The positive enrichment of ribosomal subunits including RPL31, and SRP co-translational factors (SSR1/3, SEC61α, SRPRB) located in close proximity to RPL26 suggests an involvement of UFMylation in this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and known protein interactions.

claim: Genetic ablation of UFMylation in cell culture correlates with down-regulation of proteins involved in the innate immune response following UFC1 knockdown suggesting an overall reduction in inflammation.
source: Interestingly, genetic ablation of UFMylation in cell culture reduces viral-mediated interferon production and correlates with our observed down-regulation of proteins involved in the innate immune response following UFC1 knockdown suggesting an overall reduction in inflammation (Snider et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference connecting cited literature to the current study's findings.

claim: The systems genetics and functional screening strategy provides a rich resource to explore mechanisms governing skeletal muscle metabolic function.
source: Collectively, our systems genetics and functional screening strategy provides a rich resource to further explore mechanisms governing skeletal muscle metabolic function, and we demonstrate its use by identifying UFMylation as an important modification for muscle biology.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the overall contribution of the study.

claim: UFMylation is an important modification for muscle biology.
source: Collectively, our systems genetics and functional screening strategy provides a rich resource to further explore mechanisms governing skeletal muscle metabolic function, and we demonstrate its use by identifying UFMylation as an important modification for muscle biology.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Only female mice were used in the HMDP proteomic analysis, whereas phenotypic analyses were performed on several separate cohorts using both sexes.
source: We only performed proteomics on female mice from the HMDP, whereas phenotypic analyses were performed on several separate cohorts using both sexes.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Sex interacts with common genetic variation to influence many outcomes.
source: Clearly, sex interacts with common genetic variation to influence many outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in genetics.

claim: The associations between genetic variants and proteins/phenotypes may be either causal or reactive in nature.
source: Another potential limitation of our study is that the associations between genetic variants and proteins/phenotypes may be either causal or reactive in nature.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and consideration for interpretation.

claim: A genetic variant may drive a change in protein abundance which then regulates a phenotype, or the genetic variant changes the phenotype which subsequently changes the abundance of the protein.
source: That is, a genetic variant may drive a change in protein abundance which then regulates a phenotype, or the genetic variant changes the phenotype which subsequently changes the abundance of the protein.
evidence: This is an explanation of potential causal relationships in genetic associations.

claim: Associations may have pleiotropic affects where a genetic variant may regulate the abundance of multiple proteins which modulate a phenotype either via horizontal or vertical pleiotropy.
source: Furthermore, associations may have pleiotropic affects where a genetic variant may regulate the abundance of multiple proteins which modulate a phenotype either via horizontal or vertical pleiotropy.
evidence: This is an explanation of potential pleiotropic effects in genetic associations.

claim: The results of the knockdown screen may not be relevant for the study of myogenesis and muscle regeneration.
source: Hence, the results of our screen may not be relevant for the study of myogenesis and muscle regeneration.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation regarding the interpretation of the screening results.

claim: Additional studies are warranted to investigate if the regulation of UFMylation can provide functional benefits during atrophy.
source: Furthermore, additional studies are warranted to investigate if the regulation of UFMylation can provide functional benefits during atrophy.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: rAAV6 vectors provide high tropism to terminally differentiated myofibers.
source: It is also important to note that we used rAAV6 vectors which provides high tropism to terminally differentiated myofibers (Blankinship et al., 2004) and hence, additional methodologies are required to investigate the role of UFMylation in other cell types including defective neuronal cell populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blankinship et al., 2004.

source: It is also important to note that we used rAAV6 vectors which provides high tropism to terminally differentiated myofibers (Blankinship et al., 2004) and hence, additional methodologies are required to investigate the role of UFMylation in other cell types including defective neuronal cell populations.
